I cannot account for it. It may be that the atmosphere, long since burdened by the exhalations of our mechanical age, underwent some subtle yet profound alteration; or perhaps, merely, that the human organism, in its persistent adaptability, discovered an entirely new vector for its survival. It is customary to consider human evolution as a slow, terrestrial crawl, an ascent from land to upright posture, but people, unfamiliar with the more recent conjectures of biospheric integration, forget that our very envelope of air is a vast, untrodden ocean. As such radical shifts occur, life, ever resourceful, will fill the void; and it may be that some portion of our kind had ascended to this untamed upper world. Whatever the reason, the fact remains that the very air was far more populous than we had ever conceived.

“Well, one particularly vivid morning—my second in the High Strata, I believe—as I was adjusting the graviton-lenses of my observational platform, attempting to pierce the perpetual, iridescent haze that enveloped the peaks, there happened this strange thing. Suspended above the ancient, corroded spire of what once must have been a colossal data-mast, I found a peculiar eddy in the light, whose edges seemed to shimmer with an internal luminosity. By contrast with the pervasive, diffuse glow, it seemed at first a mere trick of the eye, a vagrant distortion. I adjusted my filters, straining to resolve the indistinct form, for the change from a generalized brilliance to a pinpoint of intense light made spots of colour swim before me. Suddenly I halted, utterly transfixed. A pair of eyes, luminous by reflection against the daylight without, was watching me out of the haze.

“The old, primal awe of the truly unknown came upon me. I gripped the cold metal rail and steadfastly peered into the glaring orbs. I was afraid to turn, afraid to break the fragile communion. Then the thought of the absolute security in which humanity, at least the humanity of my sphere, appeared to be living came to my mind. And then I remembered that strange wonder at the boundless skies. Overcoming my fear to some extent, I leaned forward and spoke. I will admit that my voice was a mere whisper, thin and tremulous in the vast silence. I put out my hand, slowly, and touched nothing but cold air. At once the eyes widened slightly, and something impossibly delicate flitted past me, leaving a brief, shimmering contrail of light. I turned with my heart in my mouth, and saw a queer little winged figure, its body a translucent silver, its head held high in a peculiar manner, darting across the sunlit space behind me. It vanished into a rift of darker clouds, and in a moment was hidden within the profound obscurity.

“My impression of it is, of course, imperfect; but I know it was of a living silver, and had strange, large, purplish-black eyes; also that there was a faint, almost ethereal halo of energy surrounding its form. But, as I say, it went too fast for me to see distinctly. I cannot even say whether it possessed conventional limbs, or merely manipulated its form through subtle atmospheric currents. After an instant’s pause I strained my vision, peering into the dark rift. I could not find it at first; but, after a time in the profound obscurity, I came upon one of those vast, circular updraft currents, of which I had told you, half obscured by a churning cloud. A sudden thought came to me. Could this Thing have vanished into the current? I activated my auxiliary imager, and, looking down, I saw a small, silver, moving creature, with large bright eyes which regarded me steadfastly as it ascended. It made me shudder. It was so like a human spirit! It was flowing up the current, and now I saw for the first time a number of shimmering energy-webs, forming a kind of ladder within the updraft. Then my imager’s power flickered and failed, going out as it dropped, and when I had restarted another cycle, the little being had disappeared.

“I do not know how long I sat peering into that updraft. It was not for some time that I could succeed in persuading myself that the thing I had seen was human. But, gradually, the truth dawned on me: that Man had not remained one species, but had differentiated into two distinct organisms: that my heavy-footed people of the Terrestrial Plane were not the sole descendants of our generation, but that this delicate, ethereal, high-altitude Thing, which had flashed before me, was also heir to all the ages.

“I thought of the endless cloud-oceans and of my theory of an atmospheric metabolism. I began to suspect their true import. And what, I wondered, was this Sky-Walker doing in my scheme of a perfectly balanced ecological niche? How was it related to the ponderous, ground-bound existence of my own kind? And what was hidden up there, at the apex of that updraft? I sat upon the edge of the platform telling myself that, at any rate, there was nothing to fear, and that there I must ascend for the solution of my difficulties. And withal I was absolutely afraid to go! As I hesitated, two of my own expeditionary team came clambering in their careful ascent across the perilous rock-face in the diffused sunlight. The male assisted the female, pointing out secure handholds as they climbed.

“They seemed distressed to find me, my arm against the cold metal, peering into the cloud. Apparently it was considered bad form to remark these atmospheric phenomena; for when I pointed to this one, and tried to frame a question about it in their tongue, they were still more visibly distressed and turned away. But they were interested by my atmospheric charts, and I displayed some to amuse them. I tried them again about the updraft, and again I failed. So presently I left them, meaning to go back to my instruments, and see what I could get from them. But my mind was already in revolution; my guesses and impressions were slipping and sliding to a new adjustment. I had now a clue to the import of these updrafts, to the perpetual haze, to the mystery of the “whispering winds”; to say nothing of a hint at the meaning of the ancient spires and the fate of terrestrial man! And very vaguely there came a suggestion towards the solution of the biospheric problem that had puzzled me.

“Here was the new view. Plainly, this second species of Man was aerial. There were three circumstances in particular which made me think that its rare descent towards the lower strata was the outcome of a long-continued atmospheric habit. In the first place, there was the shimmering, almost transparent look common in most organisms that live largely in the upper air—the diaphanous wings of the High-Reaches birds, for instance. Then, those large eyes, with that capacity for gathering diffuse light, are common features of aerial things—witness the nocturnes and the cloud-moths. And last of all, that evident agility in the thin air, that hasty yet graceful flight towards thicker cloud, and that peculiar carriage of the head while in the light—all reinforced the theory of an extreme sensitivity to subtle atmospheric variations.

“Above my head, then, the sky must be traversed by these currents enormously, and these currents were the habitat of the New Race. The presence of updraft shafts and energy-webs along the cloud formations—everywhere, in fact, except along the solid peaks—showed how universal were its ramifications. What so natural, then, as to assume that it was in this ethereal Upperworld that such energy as was necessary to the comfort of the sky-dwellers was gathered? The notion was so plausible that I at once accepted it, and went on to assume the how of this splitting of the human species. I dare say you will anticipate the shape of my theory; though, for myself, I very soon felt that it fell far short of the truth.

“At first, proceeding from the problems of our own age, it seemed clear as daylight to me that the gradual widening of the present merely temporary and physical difference between the Ground-Dwellers and the Air-Born was the key to the whole position. No doubt it will seem grotesque enough to you—and wildly incredible!—and yet even now there are existing circumstances to point that way. There is a tendency to utilise higher altitudes for the less physical aspects of civilization; there is the orbital platforms in low earth orbit, for instance, there are new atmospheric cities, there are cloud-farms, there are high-altitude research stations and atmospheric purifiers, and they increase and multiply. Evidently, I thought, this tendency had increased till Humanity had gradually lost its birthright in the earth. I mean that it had gone higher and higher into larger and ever larger atmospheric structures, spending a still-increasing amount of its time therein, till, in the end! Even now, does not a High-Plateau worker live in such artificial conditions as practically to be cut off from the natural surface of the earth?

“Again, the exclusive tendency of the highly adapted—due, no doubt, to the increasing refinement of their atmospheric existence, and the widening gulf between them and the rough physicality of the ground-bound—is already leading to the mastery, in their interest, of considerable portions of the upper atmosphere. About the High Strata, for instance, perhaps half the lighter clouds are claimed against intrusion. And this same widening gulf—which is due to the length and expense of the higher atmospheric processes and the increased facilities for and temptations towards ethereal habits on the part of those best suited to such an existence—had finally led to the evolution of a truly aerial species, a creature of light and air, far above the heavy world of man.”

For if the higher atmospheric processes, with their attendant complexities and temptations towards habits of an extreme delicacy, had forged this creature of light and air, then what, I questioned, had become of that portion of humanity which had, through similar pressures, been condemned to a far more arduous and terrestrial existence? My initial impression of the ‘human spider,’ as I had, in that moment of profound revulsion, termed it, now solidified into a coherent, albeit horrifying, piece of this new, unsettling puzzle. This creature, glimpsed but fleetingly amidst the ruins, with its pallid skin and unnervingly large, reflective eyes, was not some stray beast, some aberrant mutation, but rather the perfectly adapted, albeit tragically diminished, heir to the lower stratum of that ancient divide.

It seemed to me, then, with a terrible clarity, that the economic problem, which had perplexed me but a moment before in its aerial manifestation, now presented itself in a far more stark and dreadful form. The very comfort and delicate beauty of the Air-Born, their seemingly effortless existence within the airy currents, could not, I reasoned, be sustained without some foundation, some hidden engine of production. For civilisation, however rarefied, however divorced from the grosser necessities of our own age, must still require its maintenance, its infrastructure, its steady supply of those elements which, by their very nature, are rooted in the earth, or at least in the denser strata of the atmosphere. And who, I asked myself with a growing sense of dread, was it that performed these essential, yet unglamorous, tasks? Who bore the burden of the physical, whilst the others drifted, light and free, above?

The answer, I now perceived, lay in the very phenomena which had so recently confounded me: the deep, well-like apertures, the curious structures of earth and metal which I had, even then, begun to suspect were not merely for ventilation. These were the conduits, the very arteries, of a forgotten, and indeed, deliberately obscured, existence. The creature I had seen, that fumbling, spectral thing, was, I was now utterly convinced, a representative of the true proletariat of this distant age, an animal formed and warped by the inexorable pressures of a perpetual, laborious servitude. It was the descendant of those who had, in ages past, been confined to the lower altitudes, to the ground-level work-zones, to the very surface of the planet, which the aerial race had so assiduously abandoned as ‘less ornamental.’

Their peculiar features, which had initially struck me with a primitive terror, now resolved themselves into a terrible, coherent picture of adaptive specialisation. Those large, greyish-red eyes, so unsettling in their reflective intensity, were plainly the inheritance of generations spent in conditions of perpetual gloom, or at best, in the muted, filtered light of the lower atmosphere, or indeed, the surface itself, long since overshadowed by the cities above. The extreme sensitivity to light, evinced by the creature’s swift, yet stumbling, flight towards shadow, its head held low in a manner suggestive of profound discomfort in the brilliant daylight, spoke eloquently of a retina exquisitely attuned to the faintest glimmer, but overwhelmed by the unfiltered effulgence of the sun. The pallor of its skin, a dull white, almost bleached, further confirmed this hypothesis; it was the complexion of creatures denied the vitalizing touch of the sun, analogous, I considered, to the sightless fish of abyssal caves, or those peculiar subterranean animals whose very pigments seem to have atrophied from disuse. And as for its peculiar, almost ape-like gait, and the ‘flaxen hair on its head and down its back,’ these too, I now surmised, were the outward signs of a species that had long since abandoned the graceful, upright posture of early humanity, adapting instead to an environment that demanded swift, agile movement through confined spaces, or perhaps, a posture more suited to a life lived close to the ground, or even clinging to structures.

The thought occurred to me with a fresh access of horror: if the Air-Born had, through their increasing refinement and the widening gulf of social distinction, elevated themselves to a state of almost ethereal grace, then the Ground-Dwellers, by the selfsame process, must have descended into a condition of corresponding brutishness. This was the dark obverse of the shining coin of progress, the inevitable shadow cast by the brilliant sun of their aerial civilisation. The delicate, beautiful Air-Born, in their airy cities and cloud-farms, living a life of perpetual ease and sensory delight, were, I now saw, merely the outward manifestation of a profound, and ultimately tragic, social equilibrium. For every upward step taken by the fortunate, there must be a corresponding descent, a plunge into the less desirable, more laborious spheres, by those less privileged, or less adapted to the insubstantial heights.

My mind raced, attempting to reconstruct the trajectory of this grim bifurcation. It began, I speculated, with that same increasing refinement of habits, that growing distaste for manual labour, which, in our own age, already drives the leisured classes from the workshop and the field. The desire for ease, the pursuit of beauty, the intellectualisation of existence, all these admirable human impulses, when pursued to their ultimate, unchecked conclusion, had led the ancestors of the Air-Born ever higher, away from the grime and struggle of the ground. The very atmosphere, once merely a medium for flight or a source of meteorological observation, became their dwelling place, their garden, their sanctuary from the perceived vulgarity of the earth. Gradually, over countless generations, their physical forms adapted to this new dominion: bones growing lighter, senses becoming attuned to the subtle shifts of air and light, musculature refined for minimal effort in an environment that offered little resistance. Their very souls, I dared to imagine, had grown lighter, more delicate, more attuned to the fleeting beauty of cloud and sky.

But what of those who were left behind, those who, either by inclination or by the inexorable demands of an evolving society, could not, or would not, follow their brethren into the buoyant expanse? They, I posited, remained rooted to the earth, or to its immediate vicinity, bound by the very necessities which the ascending race had sought to escape. The initial division, I conjectured, would have been purely social, a matter of class distinction: the thinkers, the artists, the refined, ascending to the clean, open skies, and the workers, the maintainers, the labourers, remaining on the surface to produce the goods, to manage the infrastructure, to harness the resources which even the most ethereal civilisation must, ultimately, consume. As the Air-Born soared ever higher, building their magnificent cloud-cities and platforms, constructing their atmospheric purifiers and energy-webs, the demand for physical labour, for the raw materials, for the intricate machinery that sustained their weightless existence, would have grown exponentially.

And so, the Ground-Dwellers, the descendants of the early working classes, found themselves increasingly confined, not by overt force perhaps, but by the relentless logic of specialisation. Their days, I surmised, were spent in the processing plants, in the ground-based mines extracting essential minerals, in the vast automated factories beneath the clouds, or perhaps in the maintenance of the complex energy grids that powered the entire aerial society. Their senses, unlike those of their sky-borne counterparts, would have adapted to the denser air, to the enclosed spaces, to the constant drone of machinery, or to the subtle vibrations of the earth itself. The sunlight, so vital and life-giving to the upper world, became an intrusion, a harsh glare that interfered with their work, or indeed, with their very physiology, which had become accustomed to the dimmer, more uniform light of their confined habitats. Their eyes, I had observed, were perfect for gathering diffuse light, for navigating by subtle reflections, for detecting movement in the shadows, but were ill-suited for the full blaze of day.

This gradual, yet relentless, process of adaptation, driven by the widening chasm between the lives of the two classes, had, in the long aeons that had elapsed, transformed them into two distinct species, each perfectly suited to its own realm, yet tragically alienated from the other. With one last glance at the retreating, shrieking Morlocks, now desperately attempting to beat out the flames, I pushed the lever forward, accelerating rapidly.

In my pocket, beyond the now precious matchbox, I found a small silver flask of brandy, which I had brought for entirely different, more convivial eventualities, and a box of safety matches, somewhat damp, but still serviceable. There was also a piece of cheese, a few biscuits, and a small, heavy iron lever, originally intended for a minor adjustment upon the machine itself. This last, I now realised, might serve a far more immediate and brutal purpose. My clothes, though somewhat travel-worn, were still stout, and my boots, though not ideal for subterranean exploration, offered some protection. I was, in short, ill-equipped for a journey into the heart of a new, unforeseen horror, but I was not entirely defenceless.

I knelt again by the lip of the well, and with a careful hand, struck a match. The tiny flame, so insignificant in the vastness of the ruins, seemed like a beacon of hope against the crushing darkness below. I held it aloft, peering into the shaft. The well, as I have described, was circular, perhaps some eight or nine feet in diameter, and the light, though feeble, revealed the glint of metal rungs, forming a crude ladder against the smooth, damp wall. The air rising from below was chill and strangely still, devoid of the gentle currents I had expected from a ventilating shaft. This, I reasoned, was not a simple chimney for air; it was a highway, a thoroughfare, a vertical channel for the nocturnal race. The implications were chilling. If it were truly a ventilating shaft, surely some natural upward draft would be discernible; its stillness suggested a sealed system, a deliberate isolation from the upper world, save for the movement of its inhabitants.

My heart still pounded with a frantic rhythm, but a certain grim determination began to assert itself. Fear, though a powerful emotion, can, when confronted with an inexorable necessity, harden into a kind of desperate courage. I took a deep breath, the air tasting faintly of earth and something else, something vaguely metallic and animalistic, which I could not then identify. I carefully inserted one foot into the opening, found the first metal rung, and began my descent.

The transition from the sunlit upper world to the profound gloom of the shaft was immediate and absolute. For a moment, even with the match held high, I was utterly blind. The blackness seemed to press in upon me, a physical weight, smothering sound and thought. The shaft echoed with the grating of my boots against the rungs, a sound strangely amplified in the confined space, and the persistent, unsettling drip of water somewhere far below. I descended slowly, cautiously, testing each rung before committing my weight. The metal was cold and slimy to the touch, and often my fingers encountered the slick, fibrous growths of some subterranean moss or fungus. The matches, though precious, were a necessity; without their flickering light, I could not have proceeded a single foot. Each one burned down rapidly, forcing me to strike another almost before the last had expired, leaving me in momentary, heart-stopping blackness between illuminations.

The descent seemed interminable. I counted the rungs, but soon lost track, the monotonous repetition blurring into an endless vertical journey. The air grew heavier, warmer, and the faint, unsettling odour I had noticed above became more pronounced, a pervasive scent of damp earth, stagnant water, and something else, a musky, mammalian smell, overlaid with a faint, cloying sweetness, like decaying vegetation. I began to hear sounds: a faint, persistent hum, like distant machinery, and occasionally, a scuttling, rustling noise, which sent a fresh wave of adrenaline through me, making me grip the cold rungs with desperate strength. My imagination, always prone to overactivity in the face of the unknown, conjured grotesque shapes in the periphery of my vision, shadows that shifted and melted back into the oppressive dark. I forced myself to maintain my composure, to rationalise each sound, to distinguish between the products of a heightened imagination and actual, tangible threats.

At length, after what felt like an hour, though it was likely far less, the shaft widened, and I found myself no longer in a confined cylinder, but at the mouth of a vast, dimly perceived cavern. The air here was warmer still, and the persistent hum of machinery, which had been a faint murmur, now became a low, pervasive thrum that resonated in my chest. I extinguished my match, not wishing to give away my position immediately, and allowed my eyes to adjust to the deeper gloom. It was not absolute darkness; a very faint, phosphorescent glow seemed to emanate from the walls themselves, a pallid, sickly luminescence that barely illuminated the immediate surroundings. I could discern monstrous shapes, huge, indistinct masses of something I could not identify, rising like petrified giants in the cavernous space.

I stood for a long moment, listening, my every sense strained. The scuttling noises were more frequent here, closer. I heard a faint, high-pitched chittering sound, followed by a soft, almost leathery rustle. It was then that my eyes, slowly adapting to the sub-faint light, caught a movement. A figure, no larger than a child, but with the disproportionate limbs and hunched posture I now associated with the subterranean race, moved swiftly across a distant, barely visible ledge. Its eyes, I could just make out, reflected the faint glow, shining like tiny, malevolent embers. It was a Morlock, and I was in its domain.

My heart gave a sickening lurch, but I forced myself to remain still, pressed against the rough-hewn rock of the well’s opening. The figure disappeared into the gloom. I waited, holding my breath, until the chittering sound had faded. I then carefully struck another match, shielding the flame as best I could with my hand, and took stock of my immediate surroundings. I was in a large, irregular chamber, its ceiling lost in the high darkness, its floor uneven and strewn with what appeared to be detritus. On one side, the wall was not rock, but a sheer face of some dark, metallic substance, pierced by numerous openings, like the mouths of tunnels. From these openings came the ceaseless thrumming, and a distinct smell of hot oil and ozone.

It was evident, then, that I had stumbled into the very heart of their subterranean world, their industrial centre, their labyrinthine hive. I moved cautiously, using the fleeting light of my matches to navigate. The floor was rough and uneven, covered in a peculiar, fibrous material that yielded slightly beneath my boots. I soon realised that much of the detritus was organic, fragments of bone, dried flesh, and other unidentifiable substances, mingled with strands of hair and discarded pieces of fabric. A horrifying suspicion began to form in my mind, a suspicion that chilled me far more profoundly than the proximity of any Morlock.

I advanced slowly, following a narrow passage that seemed to lead deeper into the metallic structure. The air grew thicker, warmer still, and the hum of machinery became a deafening roar. The passage opened into a vast, cavernous space, a veritable factory of the underworld. Here, the phosphorescent glow was stronger, emanating from strange, pulsating growths on the walls and ceiling, casting grotesque, shifting shadows. Machines of an unfamiliar design filled the space, huge, intricate constructions of metal and glass, some operating with a rhythmic clanking and grinding, others emitting a soft, insistent whine. Conveyor belts, laden with dark, unidentifiable objects, moved with relentless precision from one monstrous apparatus to another. The smell of hot oil and decay was overpowering.

And then I saw them. Morlocks, by the dozens, perhaps hundreds, toiled amidst the machinery. Their movements were swift, jerky, and efficient, their large, reflective eyes constantly scanning their surroundings, their pale, hair-covered bodies glinting in the dim, alien light. They seemed oblivious to my presence, their attention wholly focused on their labour. They were the engine of this underground world, the unseen hands that maintained the fragile balance of their existence, and, as I now understood with a horrifying clarity, the ultimate source of the Eloi's food, their clothing, their very being. My earlier theory, that the Eloi were merely the luxurious, ornamental product of an over-refined civilisation, living off the efforts of a subterranean working class, began to unravel, replaced by a far more gruesome truth.

The objects on the conveyor belts, I now perceived, were not merely "detritus." They were packages, neatly wrapped in some fibrous material, which the Morlocks were processing with a chilling efficiency. I peered closer, my stomach churning with an icy dread. The packages, I realised, were bundles of the very clothing the Eloi wore, but also, and this was the revelation that shattered my composure, they contained the remains of Eloi themselves. Bones, stripped clean, and other ghastly fragments, were being sorted, processed, reduced. The faint, cloying sweetness in the air, the musky, mammalian scent,  it was the smell of a charnel house, a vast, industrial butchery. The Eloi were not merely sustained by the Morlocks; they were the Morlocks' sustenance. The beautiful, innocent, helpless creatures of the upper world were nothing more than cattle, raised for slaughter, their lives a brief, sunlit reprieve before they descended into the maw of this subterranean horror.

This revelation, so stark and brutal, struck me with the force of a physical blow. My initial fear for my own safety momentarily receded, replaced by an overwhelming sense of revulsion and despair for the fate of humanity. This was the ultimate outcome of the social division I had speculated upon: not merely segregation, but active predation. The worker had not merely inherited the earth; he had inherited the master, and consumed him. It was a grotesque inversion of the natural order, a horrific parable of societal collapse. And the "cattle," the Eloi, were too weak, too degenerate, too intellectually atrophied even to comprehend their own terrible fate. Their "fear of the dark," their irrational reluctance to enter the wells, their terror of the Morlocks, was not an irrational superstition, but a deep-seated, instinctual terror, the last vestige of self-preservation in a species reduced to helpless prey.

I shuddered, pressing myself further into the shadows, lest one of the Morlocks, with their keen, reflective eyes, should notice my intrusion. I had to find my Time Machine. The thought of lingering in this place, breathing this foul air, witnessing this abominable industry, was unbearable. I needed to escape, not merely for my own sake, but to carry this terrible truth back to my own age, a stark warning of the potential future.

I began to move again, more purposefully now, though still with extreme caution. The factory floor was a maze of machinery, glowing fungi, and scuttling Morlocks. I realised that their movements, though quick, were somewhat erratic, not the perfectly coordinated ballet of highly intelligent beings, but more akin to the purposeful scurry of ants in a disturbed nest. This offered a sliver of hope. They were not intelligent in the human sense, but rather driven by instinct and habit, a highly specialised, almost insectile intelligence, honed by countless generations of subterranean existence.

My matchbox, I knew, was my only real defence. I considered my next move. To continue through the factory floor seemed too perilous. The sheer numbers of the Morlocks, even if individually weak, would overwhelm me. I needed to find a less populated route, a passage that might lead towards the location of my machine. I remembered the Time Machine was in a kind of pedestal, probably secured within a chamber, not openly displayed on the factory floor. It would be an object of curiosity, perhaps even a sacred object, but it was undoubtedly stored somewhere apart from their daily toil.

I began to look for side passages, smaller tunnels that branched off from the main factory complex. The phosphorescent fungi, which cast the only light, were not uniformly distributed; some areas were plunged into deeper shadow, others illuminated by a network of glowing tendrils. I found a narrow, winding tunnel, barely wide enough for me to pass through, its walls thick with the glowing moss. The air here was less acrid, and the machinery's roar faded to a distant hum. This was better. This felt less like the heart of their industry and more like a service corridor, a passage to other parts of their sprawling domain.

As I navigated the winding passage, the glowing fungi often illuminated strange, angular symbols carved into the rock walls, symbols I could not decipher, but which suggested some form of crude communication or marking. Occasionally, I would hear the faint chittering of a Morlock, or the soft pad of its feet, and I would instinctively flatten myself against the wall, holding my breath until the sound receded. Their eyesight, though keen in the dark, was clearly not adapted to detecting stationary objects, relying more on movement and perhaps, other, less human senses, such as scent or vibration. My scent, I realised with a jolt, must be an alien one to them, a strong, vibrant smell of the upper world, and one that might attract their predatory attention. I tried to move as silently as possible, suppressing every cough, every rustle of clothing.

After what felt like an age of tense, silent travel, the passage began to slope upwards. The air became cooler, and the scent of decay lessened. I could faintly discern a new odour, a familiar one, the fresh, earthy smell of the upper world, mingling with the metallic tang of the underground. Hope, a fragile, tentative thing, began to stir within me. Was I nearing the surface? Was it possible that my machine was not deep within this industrial hell, but closer to the world of light?

The passage opened into a smaller chamber, less cavernous than the factory, but still large enough to house several more of the Morlocks' incomprehensible machines. These, however, seemed different, more refined, less overtly industrial. They hummed with a softer, almost musical resonance, and were interspersed with what appeared to be crude living quarters,  hollows carved into the rock, containing piles of the fibrous material I had seen on the factory floor, likely their bedding. A few Morlocks were present, huddled together, their large eyes closed in what appeared to be a form of sleep or rest, their bodies twitching occasionally. They were clustered around a few patches of particularly bright fungi, as if seeking warmth or comfort from the light.

This, then, was likely a dormitory, or perhaps a guard post, a less active area of their domain. My caution was redoubled. I could not risk disturbing a sleeping Morlock, lest its cries alert the entire complex. I crept past the sleeping forms, my eyes scanning the chamber for any sign of my machine. I saw no pedestal, no familiar shape. The hope that had blossomed within me began to wilt.

The chamber offered several exits, narrow tunnels branching off like veins in a subterranean network. I chose one that seemed to slope further upwards, guessing that my machine, if it were near the surface, would be stored at a higher level, possibly near an access point that allowed the Morlocks to retrieve Eloi. This thought, once again, sent a shiver down my spine. The image of these creatures, emerging from their dark holes to snatch their prey, was a terrifying one.

The climb became steeper, the air colder, and the earthy scent more pronounced. I felt a definite current of fresh air, a blessed relief after the stale, acrid atmosphere of the factory. I pressed on, my muscles aching, my nerves frayed. The silence here was broken only by the occasional drip of water and my own ragged breathing.

Then, as I turned a sharp bend in the passage, I saw it. A faint, greenish glow, not the sickly phosphorescence of the fungi, but a clear, unmistakable glimmer of artificial light. My heart leaped. It was the luminescence of the Time Machine's controls! It had to be.

I quickened my pace, a surge of adrenaline overcoming my weariness. The passage opened directly into a small, irregular cave, and there, sitting precisely where I had last seen it, on its familiar green pedestal, was my Time Machine. The cave was small, almost an alcove, and the pedestal was not merely decorative, but integral to the rock, serving perhaps as a secure anchor. The controls pulsed with their customary, gentle light, a welcome beacon in this unholy darkness.

But my relief was short-lived. Between me and my machine, clustered around the pedestal like a group of macabre worshippers, were three Morlocks. They were not sleeping. They were examining the machine with an intense, almost reverent curiosity, their long, pale fingers tracing the lines of its brass and ivory, their reflective eyes glinting in its soft glow. They were smaller than I remembered, or perhaps it was the illusion of the dim light, but their presence was no less menacing. One of them, a particularly lean and agile specimen, had climbed onto the pedestal itself, running its hand along the saddle, as if trying to comprehend its purpose.

My appearance, stepping out of the shadows, startled them. They turned as one, their heads cocked, their large eyes locking onto me. For a moment, there was a tense, absolute silence, broken only by the hum of the Time Machine and my own pounding heart. Then, the chittering began, a low, agitated sound, growing in intensity. They began to advance, slowly at first, then with increasing speed, their movements fluid and predatory.

This was it. The confrontation I had dreaded. I grasped the iron lever I had brought, its cold weight a reassuring presence in my hand. With my other hand, I fumbled for my matches. There was no time for hesitation, no time for fear. Survival was everything.

I struck a match. The sudden flare of light, intense and blinding in the perpetual gloom, caused the foremost Morlock to shriek, throwing up its arms, its eyes recoiling from the glare. It staggered back, colliding with another, and for a precious instant, their attack faltered. I knew then that my primary weapon was light. Their entire existence was predicated on darkness; the sun was their enemy, and any strong illumination a miniature sun.

I advanced, holding the burning match high, its flame flickering precariously. The Morlocks retreated, their chittering turning into a series of panicked yelps. They were clearly disoriented, their superior senses of hearing and smell momentarily overwhelmed by the unexpected visual assault. I saw my opportunity. With a desperate lunge, I reached the pedestal, my hand seizing the cold, familiar lever of the Time Machine.

The Morlocks, recovering from their initial shock, began to circle, their eyes now less startled, more calculating. They were adapting, their primitive intelligence beginning to comprehend the limited range of my fiery defence. My match was burning down. I could feel the heat on my fingers. With a desperate movement, I twisted the lever. The Time Machine shuddered, its controls flaring brighter, and a faint, high-pitched whine began to emanate from its mechanism.

But the Morlocks were too swift. One of them, emboldened perhaps by the diminishing flame, leaped onto the pedestal, its clawed hand snatching at my arm. Its grip was surprisingly strong, its nails sharp, tearing at my sleeve. I cried out, more in anger than pain, and swung the iron lever with all my might. The blow connected with a sickening thud against its head. The creature collapsed, a faint, whimpering sound escaping its throat, and rolled from the pedestal.

The other two Morlocks, momentarily stunned by the sudden violence, paused. My match died, plunging us back into the semi-darkness, but the Time Machine's controls still glowed, casting their soft light. I struck another match instantly, the flare once again driving back the remaining Morlocks. They were no longer merely chittering; they were growling, a low, guttural sound that spoke of a deep-seated, animalistic rage.

I had to get away. I had activated the machine, but I needed to maintain control, to effect my departure. I needed to keep them at bay. I struck match after match, creating a flickering barrier of light around myself and the machine, but I knew my supply was limited. I was burning through them at an alarming rate.

The Morlocks, sensing my desperate plight, seemed to gain courage. They began to pelt me with small, sharp stones they picked from the cave floor, their aim surprisingly accurate. One struck my forehead, opening a shallow cut. Another grazed my cheek. The pain spurred me on. I knew I could not fight them indefinitely. My only hope was to escape, to vanish into the flow of time before they overwhelmed me.

I made a decision, a desperate one. I had to create a stronger, more lasting source of light, a temporary diversion, to give myself the few precious seconds I needed to fully activate the machine. My eyes fell upon the piles of fibrous material in the sleeping hollows. It was dry, likely flammable.

With a final, rapidly diminishing match held aloft, I made a dash for the nearest sleeping hollow. The Morlocks shrieked, darting forward, but my sudden, unexpected movement seemed to confuse them. I reached the pile of fibres, thrust the burning match into it, and watched as the dry material caught fire with an instantaneous whoosh.

Flames erupted, casting dancing, grotesque shadows across the cave walls. The Morlocks recoiled, howling in pain and fear, their pale bodies illuminated by the sudden inferno. The heat was intense, the smoke acrid, but the light was a glorious, protective barrier.

I scrambled back to my Time Machine, my heart hammering with a mixture of terror and triumph. The controls were now fully active, humming with power. I seized the main lever, the one that controlled movement through time. With one last glance at the retreating, shrieking Morlocks, now desperately attempting to beat out the flames, I pushed the lever forward, accelerating rapidly.

The cave, the Morlocks, the glowing fungi, all blurred into an indistinct smear of colour. The roar of the fire faded, replaced by the rushing wind of time. The sense of nausea, the familiar, stomach-lurching sensation of temporal displacement, swept over me. I was leaving them. I was escaping.

The journey was as swift and disorienting as my first, a kaleidoscopic whirl of light and shadow, of burgeoning cities and dissolving landscapes. I pressed the lever further, desperate to put as much time as possible between myself and that subterranean nightmare. I saw glimpses of epochs, fleeting images of a world transforming, dissolving, reforming. The sun, I noted with a detached scientific interest, had grown larger, redder, its warmth fading, its light dimming, confirming my earlier speculations about its slow, inexorable decay. The world itself seemed to be dying, covered in strange, ancient growths, blanketed by a pervasive, chilling mist.

At last, with a jolt that threw me against the saddle, I brought the machine to a halt. The temporal flux ceased. I was once more in a stable present, or rather, a stable future, but one far, far removed from the Morlocks and the Eloi. I was on a vast, flat plain, under a sky of deep crimson. The sun, a huge, dull red orb, hung low on the horizon, casting an eerie, blood-coloured light across a desolate, lichen-covered landscape. A vast, silent ocean, black and motionless, stretched to the distant horizon. The air was thin and cold, and the silence was profound, unbroken by any sound of life. Not a bird, not an insect, not a whisper of wind. The world was utterly, completely dead. My escape from the horrors of the subterranean past had led me to a different, perhaps even greater, horror, the slow, agonizing death of the very planet. But I was safe, for now. And I had my machine. The thought gave me a grim satisfaction amidst the crushing desolation. The Morlocks, I reflected, were a horror; but the ultimate, ineluctable end of all things, stretching out before me in this bleak, crimson-lit vista, was a horror of a different, more cosmic scale. And my journey, I knew, was far from over. I had seen the beginning of humanity's end, and now, I was witnessing its final, desolate stage.

These lichens, if indeed they were lichens, formed intricate, almost crystalline patterns, grey, brown, and a deep, muted purple, clinging desperately to the ancient stones that protruded here and there from the otherwise flat expanse. They were the last, forlorn vestiges of a once vibrant biosphere, enduring in a world where warmth and light were now but a memory.

The silence was, perhaps, the most profound and unnerving aspect of this terminal landscape. It was not merely the absence of sound; it was an active, palpable presence, a weight upon the senses. I listened intently, straining my ears for the faintest rustle of a leaf, the chirp of an insect, the distant cry of a bird, or even the whisper of a breeze. There was nothing. Absolutely nothing. It was as if the very air had become too thin, too cold, too utterly lifeless to carry sound. This profound quietude spoke volumes of the eons that had passed, of the slow, methodical grinding down of every intricate mechanism of life, until only this vast, cold emptiness remained. My own breath, my own heartbeat, seemed a loud, intrusive cacophony against this eternal hush.

I walked a short distance from the machine, my steps echoing only in the confines of my skull, a solitary figure dwarfed by the immensity of the dying world. My scientific impulse, however, remained stubbornly alight, a small, flickering flame in the encroaching cosmic gloom. I bent down, examining the lichen. It was unlike any terrestrial organism I had ever encountered. Its structure was impossibly complex, yet utterly rigid, a testament to a long evolution under conditions of extreme scarcity and cold. I broke off a fragment; it was brittle, dry, and crumbled to an almost impalpable powder in my gloved fingers. There was no hint of sap, no cellular moisture, no living warmth within. It was, in essence, a fossil in its own right, a living fossil of an age long past, persisting in a state of suspended animation.

My gaze swept across the horizon, seeking some variation, some feature that might offer a clue to the immense passage of time, or perhaps a final, desperate gasp of life. Far in the distance, against the blood-red disc of the sun, I thought I discerned a faint, dark silhouette. My heart, against all reason, quickened its pace. Could it be? A mountain range, perhaps, or the ruins of some unimaginably ancient civilization, a final monument to a species that had once dared to dream of permanence? The thought, however improbable, ignited a spark of my old adventurous spirit, pulling me momentarily from the abyss of despair. I resolved to investigate. This was, after all, the very purpose of my journey: to witness, to understand, to record.

I returned to the Time Machine, its familiar hum a comforting, if ultimately temporary, assertion of human ingenuity against the indifferent vastness of the universe. I consulted my instruments. The air pressure was exceedingly low, barely sufficient to sustain life for an extended period, even with my relative adaptation to various atmospheric conditions. The temperature hovered just above freezing, a stark contrast to the tropical warmth of the Eloi’s era, and a chilling harbinger of the approaching glacial night. The readings confirmed what my senses had already conveyed: this was a world on the brink of its final freeze, a planet succumbing to the heat-death of its own star.

Before setting off, I took a moment to reflect on the implications of what I had seen and was now seeing. The grand narrative of human progress, the ceaseless striving towards an enlightened future, had here met its absolute, unchallengeable rebuttal. The Morlocks and the Eloi had represented a degradation of the species, a social and biological stratification that had fractured the very essence of humanity. The sun, our life-giver, our radiant parent, would one day swell into a monstrous, crimson sphere, its light fading, its warmth dissipating, until only this cold, desolate twilight remained. The very planets would be consumed or frozen, and the universe itself, perhaps, would one day reach a similar state of ultimate, inert equilibrium. The thought was chilling, a profound and absolute negation of all purpose.

Yet, I was here. I had travelled through time. I had broken the boundaries of the present and ventured into the deep future. And despite the crushing weight of cosmic despair, the instinct for observation, for knowledge, for understanding, persisted. It was the very essence of my being, the engine that drove me forward. The silhouette on the horizon called to me, a silent challenge in the face of oblivion.

I engaged the Time Machine once more, but this time, with extreme caution. I had no desire to leap further into the desolate reaches of eternity without a purpose. My destination was that distant shape. I set the controls for a slow, measured advance through time, while simultaneously propelling the machine across the physical distance. The landscape blurred, but less dramatically than during a pure temporal jump. I could still perceive the unchanging, crimson sky, the black ocean, the vast, lichen-covered expanse. The sensation was less one of dislocation, more of a steady, deliberate glide across an infinitely patient canvas.

As I drew nearer, the indistinct form resolved itself into a more coherent shape: a series of low, irregular mounds, almost like ancient, weathered tumuli, stretching for miles across the plain. They were not artificial structures, I soon realized, nor were they mountains in the conventional sense. They seemed to be colossal, eroded rock formations, sculpted by millennia of slow, imperceptible forces, perhaps even the last vestiges of mountain ranges that had long since been worn down to their very roots. Their surfaces were covered in the same tenacious lichens, but here and there, the bare, dark stone showed through, scarred and pitted by the relentless attrition of time and the elements.

I brought the machine to a halt at the foot of one of these immense, silent monuments. The air here felt even colder, the silence more profound, as if the very presence of these ancient stones amplified the general desolation. I dismounted, my hand resting instinctively on the cold metal of my weapon, though against what enemy, I could not have said. There was nothing here that suggested a predator, nothing that hinted at life, save for the ubiquitous, tenacious lichen.

I began to climb one of the mounds, the ascent slow and arduous in the thin air and uncertain footing. My boots slipped occasionally on the loose gravel, a sound that seemed shockingly loud in the profound stillness. As I reached the summit, a panorama of an even greater bleakness unfolded before me. The plain stretched out to a vast, dark curve of the horizon, meeting the black ocean in an unbroken line. The red sun, now somewhat higher, cast a pallid, uniform glow over everything, illuminating the utterly featureless expanse.

And then I saw it. Or rather, I saw a movement. A small, dark speck, far out on the black ocean, almost at the very edge of my vision. It was difficult to discern against the dark water, but it was there, a subtle, rhythmic shift in the monotonous tableau. My scientific curiosity, momentarily dulled by the overwhelming despair, flared with renewed intensity. What could possibly move upon that inert, dying sea? Was it a last, desperate form of marine life, a creature adapted to the ultimate cold and darkness? Or was it something else, something even stranger, a final, inexplicable anomaly in the great clockwork of dissolution?

I squinted, trying to bring the distant object into sharper focus. It was too far for clear identification, even with my practiced eye. Were they but ephemeral flickers against an eternal twilight?

The thought offered a strange comfort, an anchor in the swirling chaos of temporal exploration. What if, by some unforeseen circumstance, the very fabric of this present should alter in my absence? What if the continuity I so relied upon were to unravel?

My resolve, though tested, remained firm. I had a mission, a profound, if perilous, duty. I would not merely observe the symptoms of decay, but seek its diagnosis, its aetiology, its long and tortuous progression.

The laboratory, with its familiar scent of ozone and dust, the reassuring presence of my scientific instruments, the comforting solidity of its stone walls, faded from my immediate consciousness. My mind became a vessel, poised at the edge of an unfathomable ocean, ready to launch itself into the endless currents of the fourth dimension. The silence deepened, becoming absolute, pregnant with anticipation. It was the silence of a man utterly alone, poised to confront not merely the unknown, but the *unknowable*.
